## TL;DR

Task #1056 polishes the checks progress meter from #1054/#1047: full-width pill bars on board cards, half-width meters with inline labels in the drawer and pipeline status row, and shared track/fill styling so rounding and minimum sliver width stay consistent. Pipeline cards no longer gain an extra row when progress is countable; the drawer shows the remote host once. The second review pass asked to hide the decorative native `<progress>` from assistive technology so only the styled track is announced.

## Work and rationale

Driver screenshots showed three layout problems with a common cause: native `<progress>` elements with fixed narrow widths and square caps, plus surface-specific markup that fought the desired grid. The board card capped the checks block at 320px, so the bar never reached the card’s inner edge and sat tight against the status line. The drawer pinned the meter to roughly 120px while centering the fraction label awkwardly to its right, and duplicated machine identity in both the scope line and the footer (`on remote host · remote host`). The pipeline placed progress on its own row under the status line, increasing card height.

The fix centers on `ChecksProgressDisplay.vue` with global `.check-progress-meter` rules in `style.css`. A custom track and fill deliver pill caps (`border-radius: 999px`), a 6px-tall bar, and `min-width: 6px` on the fill so values below 2% still show a visible sliver (`fillPercent` clamps displayed width to at least 2%). Layout modifiers split concerns: `--full` stretches the meter on cards; `--half` takes 50% flex basis on drawer bar rows and pipeline status rows, with detail or pipeline status text in the remaining half (ellipsis on pipeline text). Card variant uses column layout with 7px gap between bar and status line; drawer footer now only prefixes machine once via `drawerFooter` (`on ${machineLine}`) while scope line omits redundant host copy.

`TaskCard.vue`, `TaskDrawer.vue`, and `PipelineCard.vue` were trimmed to delegate markup to the shared component; pipeline integrates the meter into the existing status row instead of `pl-row-3`. Tests cover minimum fill width, drawer row layout, pipeline inline status, and (after review) a single exposed `role="progressbar"` with `aria-hidden="true"` on the sr-only native `<progress>` kept for DOM parity with older tests.

## Approaches tried

The first iteration reused native `<progress>` for semantics and layered a styled track on top, clipping the native element with a screen-reader-only class. That preserved legacy test selectors but left two progress roles in the accessibility tree. Review rejected that pairing. Adding `aria-hidden="true"` on the native element keeps it for tests and visual-offscreen fallback while the custom track owns `role="progressbar"` and `aria-valuenow`/`aria-valuemin`/`aria-valuemax`.

Width strategy uses flex on half-width surfaces rather than fixed pixel widths so narrow viewports still split 50/50 without overflow; pipeline status text uses truncation classes in global CSS.

## Challenges and blockers

Vue scoped styles from an earlier task had isolated `.check-progress` to the drawer, starving the card of meter styling until rules moved global—mostly pre-#1056 history, but it informed keeping all meter tokens in `style.css`. Pipeline shot fixtures required the meter inside the status row so `pipeline:checksProgress` highlights resolve; moving DOM without breaking `PipelineCard` row grid took a careful read of existing `pl-row-*` structure.

No human-only verification was needed; shot fixtures `card:checksProgress`, `drawer:checksProgress`, and `pipeline:checksProgress` seed countable progress for review captures.

## Key learnings

When replacing native controls with custom visuals, pick one accessibility exposure path up front: either style the native element or decorate a single ARIA widget and explicitly hide the redundant node from AT. Visually hidden (`clip`) CSS does not remove native `<progress>` from screen readers. Shared display components pay off when three surfaces must look identical but lay out differently—variant props plus BEM-style layout classes beat duplicated markup in each parent.
